Content:
Let's take a look at the following algebraic expression:
[MATH: 2x{\,\color{red}{-}\,} 4y {\,\color{blue}{+}\,} 7]
The addition [MATH: ({\color{blue}{+}})] and subtraction [MATH: ({\color{red}{-}})] symbols separate this expression into three parts known as terms.

Content:
To identify each term, we put an addition symbol [MATH: ({\color{blue}{+}})] between each part and separate using parentheses:

Content:
[MATH: (2x) {\,\color{blue}{+}\,} ({\,\color{red}{-}\,} 4y) {\,\color{blue}{+}\,} (7).]

Content:
So, the terms of this expression are:
[MATH: 2x,\quad -4y,\quad \quad 7]
We say that [MATH: 2x] is the first term, [MATH: -4y] is the second term, and [MATH: 7] is the third term.

Content:
In this example, the subtraction symbol gave us the term [MATH: -4y]. Whenever there is a subtraction symbol, the corresponding term will be negative.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's take a look at the following algebraic expression:
[MATH: 2x{\,\color{red}{-}\,} 4y {\,\color{blue}{+}\,} 7]
The addition [MATH: ({\color{blue}{+}})] and subtraction [MATH: ({\color{red}{-}})] symbols separate this expression into three parts known as terms.

Content:
To identify each term, we put an addition symbol [MATH: ({\color{blue}{+}})] between each part and separate using parentheses:

Content:
[MATH: (2x) {\,\color{blue}{+}\,} ({\,\color{red}{-}\,} 4y) {\,\color{blue}{+}\,} (7).]

Content:
So, the terms of this expression are:
[MATH: 2x,\quad -4y,\quad \quad 7]
We say that [MATH: 2x] is the first term, [MATH: -4y] is the second term, and [MATH: 7] is the third term.

Content:
In this example, the subtraction symbol gave us the term [MATH: -4y]. Whenever there is a subtraction symbol, the corresponding term will be negative.

---

So, the expression has three terms: [MATH: 3x], [MATH: 2y], and [MATH: -4x.]

Item 10 — Tutorial: Equivalent Expressions

Content:
When two algebraic expressions contain exactly the same terms, they are said to be equivalent.

Content:
For example, the expression
[MATH: {\color{blue}{x}} + {\color{red}{2y}} + 3z]
is equivalent to
[MATH: 3z+{\color{blue}{x}} + {\color{red}{2y}}]
because they both contain the exact same terms. Both expressions are also equivalent to

Content:
[MATH: {\color{blue}{x}} + 3z+ {\color{red}{2y}}.]

---
